title: Sudden oxygen desaturation
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Go to the patient first when the saturation alarm sounds and assess breathing, not just the number.
Stay with the patient, support oxygenation as the unit policy allows and clear secretions only when there is a need.
Escalate early if the saturation does not recover, then reassess and document the response.

AARC oxygen CPG: oxygen use, monitoring

Unit's pneumothorax, chest-drain malfunction, and tension-physiology emergency escalation protocol for patients on respiratory support.
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
RCUK adult ABCDE guidance now supports immediate assessment, threat recognition and reassessment. The fictional sequence is not a validated ICU-specific protocol.
Oxygen flow, targets and device choice are deliberately not written; they come from the order and policy.
Escalation score thresholds are local and are not written.

The pleural emergency differential was strengthened without adding an independently validated tension pneumothorax diagnosis or invasive procedure: specific thoracic emergencies require local ICU/pleural-team protocols and specialist sign-off.

setting: A fictional adult in a fictional intensive care unit who is breathing without a ventilator, receiving oxygen as prescribed.

steps.info: An adult without an artificial airway was talking comfortably ten minutes earlier. The saturation alarm now sounds, the patient appears anxious and the respiratory rate and effort have increased. The probe signal has not yet been checked.
steps.prompt: What should the nurse prioritize when a low saturation reading accompanies new respiratory distress?

options.text: Stay at the bedside; assess airway, breathing effort, chest symmetry, colour, lung sounds and circulation. Activate urgent help now; check oximeter reliability in parallel.
options.feedback: A rapid fall in oxygen saturation requires patient-first assessment, not an assumption of probe failure. Chest asymmetry or circulatory instability may indicate a pleural or other emergency needing immediate team assistance; oxygen readings must be interpreted with the clinical findings. Poor peripheral circulation and skin pigmentation may affect oximetry accuracy. Assess signal reliability in parallel and seek further measurement if the clinical picture is discordant; do not delay care. The RCUK adult ABCDE approach emphasizes early emergency assistance and addressing immediate threats during breathing assessment. Do not await chest imaging before escalating possible tension physiology; definitive intervention belongs to the trained team.
options.consequence: Direct patient assessment and urgent help may reveal a respiratory emergency even if the oximeter signal is unreliable; secretions are only one possibility, and the team must consider other causes of deterioration.

options.text: Reposition the oximeter probe and record the new signal quality, then leave the bedside while waiting for the displayed saturation to recover before reassessing breathing and requesting help.
options.feedback: Checking the probe can help establish signal reliability, but leaving a visibly deteriorating patient without assessing breathing is unsafe. Remain with the patient, reassess promptly and summon help.
options.consequence: Leaving to await a better signal could delay recognition of worsening respiratory failure.

options.text: Pause the audible alarm because the patient can still talk, record the earlier saturation and continue the scheduled observations without assessing the new distress or calling for urgent help.
options.feedback: A patient who can talk can still be hypoxic; early signs of hypoxia include anxiety and restlessness, and the alarm is a call to assess.
options.consequence: Being able to speak could falsely reassure the nurse while oxygenation or ventilation deteriorates.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint, the oxygen device is connected and the patient has a weak, wet cough with audible secretions. Saturation is still below the earlier baseline and respiratory effort remains increased. No single cause has been established.
steps.prompt: How should the nurse address possible retained oral secretions while investigating persistent respiratory compromise?

options.text: Activate urgent help; continue authorised oxygen and reassessment. Assess retained oral secretions; trained staff use indicated non-invasive oral suction per policy without delaying emergency assessment.
options.feedback: This fictional patient is breathing without an artificial airway. Open RN Nursing Fundamentals describes oral suction for retained mouth or pharyngeal secretions. The AARC artificial-airway guideline does not establish suction technique for this patient. Escalate ongoing respiratory compromise and reassess the response.
options.consequence: Indicated secretion clearance and urgent reassessment may improve airway patency while allowing the team to investigate other causes.

options.text: Repeat suction whenever the displayed saturation remains below baseline, without reassessing secretion clearance, tolerance or other causes, and defer emergency assessment until the saturation has returned to its earlier level.
options.feedback: Repeating suction without reassessing indication, patient tolerance and the cause of deterioration is unsafe. Suction is not a substitute for urgent clinical assessment.
options.consequence: Repeated suction without reassessment could worsen distress or delay treatment of another respiratory emergency.

options.text: Increase oxygen or change devices solely to restore the previous monitor reading, recording the response without reassessing breathing or using the authorised emergency escalation pathway.
options.feedback: Emergency oxygen and breathing support must not be withheld when indicated. Use the authorized emergency pathway, assess the cause and reassess the patient; do not chase a displayed saturation alone.
options.consequence: A higher displayed saturation could conceal ongoing respiratory compromise if the patient is not reassessed.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, the responding team is at the bedside. Saturation has risen from 86% to 91%, but respiratory effort is still increased and heart rate remains fast. Improvement in one reading has not established recovery.
steps.prompt: What handover and reassessment are needed despite the partial improvement in saturation?

options.text: Give SBAR on findings, actions and response; continue monitoring heart rate, breathing, saturation, lung sounds and breathlessness. Document interventions and effects.
options.feedback: Reassessment after an intervention includes heart rate, breathing rate, oximetry and lung sounds and asking the patient to rate breathlessness; the effect of interventions is documented. Document oxygen device and delivered oxygen concentration where known, and communicate respiratory effort as well as saturation. Pulse oximetry does not measure carbon dioxide; persistent respiratory distress despite improved saturation needs urgent reassessment, with blood gas assessment as indicated.
options.consequence: A clear timeline and reassessment may help the team recognize persistent respiratory compromise and evaluate the response to treatment.

options.text: Step back and let the team work without giving a structured handover of the recent changes or confirming ongoing reassessment, and plan to reconstruct the event in the notes later.
options.feedback: With continued increased breathing effort, stepping away without a structured transfer of responsibility risks missed deterioration. Provide the responding team with the timeline and ensure ongoing assessment.
options.consequence: Stepping away could leave essential findings uncommunicated and monitoring responsibility unclear.

options.text: Reset the alarm limits to stop audible alerts during the team's treatment, then document the improved saturation without reporting the persistent increased breathing effort or agreeing ongoing monitoring.
options.feedback: Alarm limits are set according to the order or protocol; widening limits during an event hides further change.
options.consequence: Changing limits could hide subsequent deterioration instead of addressing its cause.

learning_points: Go to the patient first: assess the airway, breathing effort, colour, lung sounds and heart rate, and use the oximeter reading as one finding among others.

Stay with the patient, support oxygenation within authorised policy and consider oral secretion clearance only when indicated and within trained scope. Artificial-airway suction techniques do not apply to this case.
Escalate early when the saturation does not recover, and reassess the same parameters after every intervention.
Do not silence alarms or change limits and devices without authority; hand over with SBAR and document the response.

A wet cough does not exclude pneumothorax, an obstructed drain, or other causes of deterioration. New asymmetric chest movement, hypotension or severe respiratory compromise requires urgent skilled response; do not delay for device adjustments or chest radiography.
Poor perfusion or pigmentation-related measurement limitations may affect oximetry; evaluate the patient and signal together, and obtain further assessment when findings disagree.
